title: Organic Skincare & Hair Products
subtitle: Make, test, cost and honestly sell whipped shea butter, body oils, hair oils and balms that are safe and consistent.
description: A practical course for women who want to make natural skin and hair products to a professional standard. You will learn what each butter, oil and wax does, how to work hygienically and dilute essential oils safely, and how to make whipped shea butter, oils and balms. You will also learn why lotions need real preservatives, how to write honest labels, the basics of NAFDAC registration, and how to cost and price your products.
outcomes: Make smooth whipped shea butter, body oils, hair and scalp oils and beeswax balms from written, weighed formulas
Calculate essential oil amounts within recognised dilution limits and work hygienically
Explain why water-based products need a broad-spectrum preservative and avoid unsafe recipes
Run skin tests and user trials, keep batch records and set a defensible best-before date
Write honest claims and a correct label, and outline NAFDAC registration steps
Cost a product fully and set retail and wholesale prices
audience: Women who already make or want to make natural skin and hair products at home and want to sell them safely and professionally.
tools: Digital kitchen scale (1 g) and a small pocket scale (0.01 g)
Heat-safe bowls, a pot for a double boiler, spatulas and a hand mixer
70% alcohol, gloves, apron and paper towels
Shea butter, liquid oils (for example coconut, olive, castor), beeswax and optional essential oils
Clean jars, amber bottles, tins and labels
Smartphone with WhatsApp and a notebook or Google Sheets for records

modules.title: Foundations: products, ingredients and safety
modules.overview: Before you melt anything, you need to know which products a small home maker can make safely, what each butter, oil and wax actually does, and how to keep your work clean and your essential oils at safe levels. This module gives you that base.

lessons.title: Which natural skin and hair products you can make safely at home
objectives: Explain the difference between water-free (anhydrous) and water-based products
Name the four product types this course teaches and what each is for
Explain why this course does not teach home lotions without proper preservatives
Describe where handmade natural products fit in the Nigerian market

blocks.text: This course teaches four products that a careful beginner can make well in a home kitchen: **whipped shea butter**, **body oils**, **hair and scalp oils**, and **simple balms** made with beeswax. All four have one thing in common: they contain **no water**. Makers call these products **anhydrous**, which simply means water-free.

blocks.name: lotion-bottle
blocks.alt: A pump bottle of body product
blocks.caption: Lotions look simple, but because they contain water they need a proper preservative, which is why we start with water-free products.

blocks.text: Why water changes everything

Bacteria, yeast and mould need water to grow. A jar of pure shea butter or a bottle of oil gives them almost nothing to live on, so oil-only products do not need a preservative to stay safe from germs. Their main enemy is **rancidity**: oils slowly react with air, light and heat and begin to smell like old groundnuts or crayons. You slow that with fresh ingredients, clean dry containers, and storage away from sun.

A lotion or cream is different. It is a mix of oil and water held together by an emulsifier. The moment water is present, germs can grow, often without any smell or colour change you can see. Formulation teachers such as Humblebee & Me state plainly that anything containing water needs a **broad-spectrum preservative** unless it is used up immediately. That includes products made with aloe vera juice, rose water (a hydrosol), milk or herbal teas. Module 3 explains this fully. For now, the rule is simple: if it has water in it, it needs a real preservative and proper training.

blocks.title: Water-free versus water-based products
items: Water-free (anhydrous)
Water-based (emulsions, sprays)
blocks.caption: Starting with water-free products removes the biggest safety risk while you build skill.

blocks.text: The four products in this course

head: Product
Main ingredients
What customers use it for
rows: Shea butter plus a liquid oil, whipped until light and fluffy
Rich moisture for dry skin, elbows, feet, and as a hair butter for sealing moisture into natural hair

blocks.text: Notice what is not on the list: bleaching creams, "strong" toning products, anything with hydroquinone, mercury or steroids, and medicated products. Those are either illegal in cosmetics, dangerous, or fall under drug rules. A natural products maker builds trust by staying far away from them.
Where this fits in the Nigerian market

Shea butter is not new to us. It comes from the nut of the shea tree (Vitellaria paradoxa), which grows across the savannah belt of West Africa, including northern Nigeria. In Yoruba it is called **ori**, and many families already use raw shea on skin and hair. Your value as a maker is not that you discovered shea. It is that you turn good raw ingredients into a product that is **clean, consistent, pleasant to use, honestly labelled and attractively packed**.

items: Customers who wear their hair natural buy oils and butters often, because they use them every wash day.
Mothers look for gentle, simple, unperfumed products for their families.
Gift buyers want neat jars with clear labels for birthdays, weddings and end-of-year packages.
Salons and small shops may stock a few local products if the quality is steady and the label is professional.

blocks.title: Worked example: choosing a first product line
blocks.context: For example, Ngozi in Enugu already sells provisions from a small shop and wants to add natural products. She has about ₦40,000 (approximate) to start.
steps: She lists what her regular customers ask for: shea butter for children, hair oil, and lip balm.
She chooses three water-free products only: unscented whipped shea, a scalp oil, and a lip and skin balm.
She decides not to make lotion until she has learnt preservation properly, even though lotion is popular.
She plans small test batches of about 300 to 500 g each so a mistake does not waste much money.
blocks.result: Ngozi starts with three safe, related products that share ingredients (shea, oils, beeswax), so she buys fewer items and wastes less.

blocks.title: Natural does not mean harmless
blocks.text: Plants can irritate skin and cause allergies, and some essential oils are strong chemicals. Natural products still need clean work, correct amounts and patch testing. This course teaches each of those.

By the end of this course you will have a written, tested formula for at least one hair product, batch records, a costing sheet, a correct label draft and a plan for the next 90 days. Keep a notebook or a folder on your phone just for this course: you will use it in every lesson.

takeaways: Water-free (anhydrous) products are the safest first products for a home maker.
Anything containing water needs a broad-spectrum preservative and proper training.
The main risk for oil products is rancidity, slowed by fresh ingredients, dry containers and cool, dark storage.
Your value is clean, consistent, honestly labelled products, not secret ingredients.

activity.title: Map your first product line
steps: Ask five people you know which natural skin or hair products they buy and how often.
Write down the three products they mention most.
Mark each as water-free or water-based.
Choose up to three water-free products to start with.
Note which ingredients the three products share.
activity.evidence: A one-page note (photo or phone note) showing the survey answers and your chosen three products.

lessons.title: Know your ingredients: butters, oils and waxes for skin and hair
objectives: Describe what shea butter, cocoa butter, coconut oil, castor oil, olive oil, jojoba and beeswax each do in a product
Tell the difference between light and heavy oils and when to use each
Match ingredients to skin and hair needs
Judge the quality and freshness of raw ingredients in the market

blocks.text: Every product in this course is built from three families of ingredients: **butters** (solid at room temperature), **liquid oils**, and **waxes**. Once you understand what each family does, you can design a formula on purpose instead of copying a recipe you do not understand.

blocks.name: coconut
blocks.caption: Coconut oil is a common local base oil; it turns solid when the weather is cool.

blocks.text: Butters: the body of the product

**Shea butter** is the star. It is soft, rich and melts close to skin temperature, so it spreads easily and leaves a protective feel. Unrefined shea is ivory to yellowish with a nutty, smoky smell. Refined shea is whiter with little smell. Both work; unrefined keeps more of its natural character. **Cocoa butter** is much harder and has a chocolate smell; a little of it makes balms firmer. Mango butter is another soft butter, but it is usually imported and costs more.
Liquid oils: light, medium and heavy

Oils feel very different on skin and hair. A **light** oil sinks in quickly and leaves little shine. A **heavy** oil is thick, stays on the surface longer and feels greasier. Good formulas usually blend one heavier oil with one or two lighter ones.

head: Oil
Feel
Notes for skin and hair
rows: Popular and local. Some people find it clogs facial pores. Many people with natural hair like it for pre-wash oiling.
Easy to find. Rich feel on skin; a little goes a long way in hair blends.
Very thick, so use as a smaller part of a blend. Used a lot in hair products for coating and shine.
Technically a liquid wax, close in structure to the oil our skin makes. Good for scalp and face but usually imported and costly.
Silky body oil. It comes from a tree nut, so warn customers with nut allergies.
Traditional hair oil in parts of Nigeria (often dark, with a strong smell). Different from red palm oil.

blocks.text: Waxes: the structure

**Beeswax** turns oils into a solid balm. It melts at roughly 62 to 64 °C, much higher than shea, so balms made with it stay firm in the heat. More wax makes a harder balm; less wax makes a softer salve. Beeswax is an animal product, so it is not vegan; candelilla wax is a plant alternative but harder to find.

blocks.title: How a balm or butter is built
items: Essential oil: tiny amount, scent
Liquid oils: spread and softness
Butters: richness and body
Wax: structure (balms only)
blocks.caption: Most of the product is butter and oil; the scent is only a very small part at the top.

blocks.text: Skin needs versus hair needs

Skin and hair need different things. Dry skin likes richer butters that leave a protective layer. A scalp, which has many oil glands and follicles, usually prefers lighter oils that do not sit as a heavy coat. The lengths and ends of tightly coiled hair, which dry out easily, often enjoy heavier oils and butters to seal in moisture after water or a water-based leave-in has been applied. This is the idea behind the "sealing" step many people with natural hair use.

Be honest about what oils do. Oils soften, add shine, reduce friction when combing and help slow moisture loss. They do not feed hair from the outside, and there is no strong proof that any home oil blend makes hair grow faster. You will hear claims about castor oil and rosemary oil for growth. Treat them as popular beliefs, not promises.

blocks.title: Worked example: matching oils to a need
blocks.context: For example, Amina in Kaduna wants a scalp oil for customers whose scalp feels dry and tight, but who hate a greasy feel.
steps: She picks a light main oil for most of the blend: she tests jojoba, and also a cheaper option of fractionated coconut oil from a supplier.
She adds castor oil but keeps it to about 20 to 25% of the blend because it is so thick.
She adds olive oil as a middle oil for the rest.
She rubs a few drops of each version on the back of her hand and on a small area of scalp, and notes which feels least greasy after 30 minutes.
blocks.result: She now has two versions of a scalp oil with a clear reason for every ingredient, ready for proper testing in Module 2.

blocks.text: Buying quality ingredients

items: Buy from sellers who can tell you where the oil came from and when it was made or packed.
Smell before you buy: fresh oils smell mild or of their source. A sharp, paint-like or old-groundnut smell means rancid.
Raw shea should not contain sand, bits of shell or a sour smell. Ask to see inside the container.
Avoid oils sold in reused containers that once held chemicals.
Buy amounts you will use within a few months, and store them cool and away from sunlight.

blocks.title: Start a supplier sheet
blocks.text: For every ingredient, record the seller, the price, the date bought and what it smelled and looked like. When a batch turns out well or badly, this sheet helps you find out why.

takeaways: Butters give body, oils give spread and softness, wax gives structure.
Blend heavy oils (castor) with lighter ones so products do not feel sticky.
Scalps often prefer lighter oils; dry ends often like heavier oils and butters for sealing.
Oils soften and protect hair; do not promise growth.
Smell and inspect every ingredient before you buy.

activity.title: Ingredient feel test
steps: Collect small amounts of three oils you can buy locally (for example coconut, olive, castor).
Put two drops of each on a separate area of your forearm and rub in.
After 10 minutes and 30 minutes, write how greasy, shiny and soft each area feels.
Rank the oils from lightest to heaviest.
Note the price per litre of each oil from your market.
activity.evidence: A small table in your notebook or phone with each oil, its feel at 10 and 30 minutes, its rank and price.

lessons.title: Hygiene, safe working and essential oil dilution limits
objectives: Set up a clean, sanitised work area and equipment
Calculate the amount of essential oil for a safe dilution by weight
Apply recognised dilution ranges for face, body and sensitive skin
Recognise essential oils that need extra care

blocks.text: Two habits separate a professional maker from a hobbyist: **clean work** and **measured strength**. This lesson covers both. Even water-free products can pick up germs if water or dirty fingers get in, and essential oils can burn or sensitise skin if they are used too strong.

blocks.name: gloves
blocks.caption: Gloves and clean tools keep your hands and germs out of the product.

blocks.text: Setting up a clean workspace

items: Clear the table of food, pets and children. Tie back hair and wear an apron.
Wash the table, then wipe it with 70% alcohol (isopropyl or ethanol) and let it dry.
Wash bowls, spatulas, whisks and jars with hot soapy water, rinse well and dry completely.
Spray or wipe tools and the inside of jars with 70% alcohol and let them air-dry fully before use. The alcohol must evaporate; it should not be wet when you fill.
Wear clean gloves and do not touch your face or phone while working.
Keep a dedicated set of tools for products only, not for cooking.

blocks.text: **Dry is as important as clean.** A single drop of water left in a jar gives germs a place to start. Customers also add water when they dip wet fingers into a jar in the bathroom, which is why it helps to give a small spatula or recommend clean dry hands.

blocks.title: Clean work routine before every batch
items: Clear and wash surface
Wash and dry tools
Sanitise with 70% alcohol
Let everything air-dry
Gloves on, then weigh
blocks.caption: Follow the same order every time so no step is forgotten.

blocks.text: What essential oils are

Essential oils are very concentrated aromatic extracts from plants, usually made by steam distillation or, for citrus peels, by pressing. A small bottle can represent a large amount of plant material. They are not the same as carrier oils such as olive or coconut, which are gentle fatty oils. Essential oils must always be diluted in a carrier before they touch skin.
Safe dilution ranges

The Tisserand Institute, founded by essential oil safety author Robert Tisserand, publishes dilution guidance used widely by aromatherapists. Its general ranges are below. Stay at the lower end when you are not sure, and remember that a nice smell does not need high strength.

For scalp oils, which sit on the skin for hours and are used often, this course takes a cautious approach and stays at 1% or below. For products meant for babies and young children, leave essential oils out completely unless you are following a specialist source; unscented products are a strong selling point for mothers anyway. Advise pregnant customers to check with their health worker before using scented products.
Calculating by weight

Dilution means the percentage of the total product weight. The easiest and most accurate way is to weigh with a small digital scale that reads to 0.01 g (often sold as a jewellery or pocket scale). Drops are a rough backup only: the Tisserand Institute notes that drop conversions are always approximate because drop size varies by oil and bottle.

blocks.title: Worked example: 2% lavender in a body butter
blocks.context: For example, Funke in Ibadan is making 250 g of whipped shea butter for adult body use and wants a light lavender scent.
steps: She chooses 2%, inside the 1 to 3% body range.
Essential oil needed: 250 g x 2 / 100 = 5 g.
The other 245 g is her butter and oil blend.
She places the bowl on the scale, presses tare (zero), and adds lavender drop by drop until the scale shows 5.00 g.
She records "Lavender 5 g, 2%" on her batch sheet.
blocks.result: Her butter is pleasantly scented and within the recognised body range. If she later made a face balm of the same size, 1% would mean only 2.5 g.

blocks.text: Oils that need extra care

items: **Tea tree, peppermint, cinnamon, clove, oregano and thyme** are known skin irritants. Never use them undiluted and keep them at low levels.

**Cold-pressed citrus oils** such as lemon, lime and bergamot can cause phototoxic burns on sunny skin. IFRA (the fragrance industry standards body) sets a 2% maximum for cold-pressed lemon in leave-on products. For products used in our sun, choose steam-distilled versions or other oils.
**Old, oxidised oils** irritate more. Keep bottles tightly closed, cool and dark, and note the opening date.
Keep peppermint and eucalyptus away from the faces of babies and small children.

blocks.title: Allergy can be permanent
blocks.text: Using essential oils too strong can cause allergic contact dermatitis. Once a person becomes allergic to an oil, they are likely to react to it every time afterwards. Low, measured dilution protects your customers and your name.

Finally, label your bottles, store all oils out of reach of children, and never let anyone swallow essential oils. A small child drinking a bottle is a medical emergency; take them to a hospital immediately with the bottle.

takeaways: Clean, sanitise with 70% alcohol, and let everything dry before filling.
Weigh essential oils on a 0.01 g scale; drops are only approximate.
Face 0.5 to 1.2%, body 1 to 3%, sensitive skin 0.2 to 1% (Tisserand Institute).
Tea tree, peppermint, clove and cinnamon irritate; cold-pressed citrus can burn in sunlight.
Leave essential oils out of baby products.

activity.title: Dilution calculation sheet
steps: Write down three products you plan to make and their batch size in grams.
Choose a dilution for each from the table, with a reason.
Calculate the grams of essential oil for each batch.
Set up your workspace using the five-step routine and take a photo of it ready to work.
activity.evidence: Your calculation sheet with three worked dilutions and a photo of your clean workspace.

quiz.q: Kemi wants to add aloe vera juice to her shea butter to make it "lighter". What changes about her product?
options: Nothing, aloe is natural so no preservative is needed
It now contains water, so it needs a broad-spectrum preservative
It will only need more vitamin E
quiz.explain: Aloe vera juice is mostly water. Once water is present, germs can grow, so the product needs a proper broad-spectrum preservative.

quiz.q: How much essential oil is needed for 300 g of body butter at 2%?
Which dilution is most suitable for a face balm, according to the Tisserand Institute ranges?
quiz.explain: The range for face products is 0.5 to 1.2%, so about 1% fits.

quiz.q: Why should castor oil usually be a smaller part of a hair oil blend?
options: It is illegal in high amounts
It is very thick and sticky, so a lot of it feels heavy
quiz.explain: Castor oil is very heavy. Blending it with lighter oils gives a nicer feel.

quiz.q: Tunde sanitised his jars with 70% alcohol. When should he fill them?
options: Immediately while still wet, so germs cannot enter
After the alcohol has fully evaporated and the jars are dry
After rinsing them with tap water
Only after boiling them in the product
quiz.explain: Jars must be completely dry. Alcohol needs to evaporate first, and rinsing with tap water would add water back.

quiz.q: A customer plans to use a lemon-scented body oil before going out in the afternoon sun. What is the concern?
options: Cold-pressed lemon oil can cause phototoxic burns on sun-exposed skin
Lemon oil makes oils go solid
quiz.explain: Cold-pressed citrus oils are phototoxic. IFRA limits cold-pressed lemon to 2% in leave-on products.

modules.title: Guided practice: whipped butter, oils and balms
modules.overview: Now you make the products. You will whip shea butter that stays smooth, blend body and hair oils with a reason for every ingredient, pour a firm balm, and then test what you made properly on yourself and others before anyone pays for it.

lessons.title: Making smooth whipped shea butter step by step
objectives: Write a whipped butter formula in percentages and convert it to grams
Melt, cool and whip shea butter to a light, stable texture
Prevent and fix grainy shea butter
Fill and store jars hygienically

blocks.text: Whipped shea butter is often the first product a natural maker sells, and also the one that shows quality most clearly. Good whipped butter is light, smooth, holds its shape in the jar and melts easily on skin. Poor whipped butter is gritty, collapses into a greasy puddle, or smells stale. The difference is method, not secret ingredients.

blocks.name: jar
blocks.caption: Whipped butter is filled into clean, completely dry jars once it is light and fluffy.

blocks.text: Write the formula in percentages first

Professionals write formulas as percentages of the total weight, then convert to grams for each batch size. That way you can make 200 g or 2 kg and the product stays the same. A simple, reliable whipped butter is about **70% shea butter and 30% liquid oil**, with essential oil (if any) taking a small part of the oil share.

More liquid oil gives a softer, more greasy-feeling butter that may slump in hot weather. Less liquid oil gives a stiffer butter. In very hot places or seasons, reduce the liquid oil a little; during harmattan, when coconut oil hardens, you may increase it slightly. Change one thing at a time and record it.
Why shea butter goes grainy

Shea butter contains several different fats that melt and set at different temperatures. If melted shea cools slowly, or is heated and cooled again and again (for example, sitting in a hot shop by day and a cool room at night), some of those fats set first and form small hard crystals. Customers feel these as grains or little lumps that melt on the skin. They are not dirt and not dangerous, but they make your product look poorly made.

The common fix used by formulators is **tempering**: melt the butter completely, keep it fully melted for a while so every crystal disappears, then cool it **quickly** so all the fats set together in a fine, smooth structure.

blocks.title: Smooth whipped shea method
items: Weigh all ingredients
Melt gently, fully liquid
Cool fast to soft-set
Whip until fluffy
Fill dry jars, label
blocks.caption: Fully melting and then cooling quickly is what prevents graininess.

blocks.text: The method

items: Clean and sanitise your workspace and tools, then let them dry (Module 1, Lesson 3).
Weigh the shea butter and coconut oil into a heat-safe bowl.

Melt over a pot of gently simmering water (a double boiler). Keep the heat low; shea should never smoke or boil. Stir until there are no solid bits at all, then keep it melted for about 10 more minutes while stirring.
Take the bowl off the heat and add the olive oil.

Cool quickly: set the bowl in a larger bowl of cold water with some ice, or place it in the fridge, stirring every few minutes. Stop when the edges are firm and the middle is like soft custard or thick pap.
Add the weighed essential oil now, when the butter is cool, so less scent evaporates.
Whip with a hand mixer for 5 to 10 minutes, scraping the sides, until the butter is pale, light and holds soft peaks. If it stays soft, chill for 10 minutes and whip again.
Spoon or pipe into clean, dry jars, tap to remove air pockets, close and label with the batch number and date.

blocks.title: Worked example: rescuing a grainy batch
blocks.context: For example, Bisi in Lagos made 1 kg of whipped butter. After two weeks in her shop by a sunny window, customers said it felt sandy.
steps: She takes back the unsold jars and checks the batch record: she had cooled the first batch slowly overnight at room temperature.
She scoops the butter into a bowl, melts it fully over low heat and holds it melted for 10 minutes.
She cools it in a bowl of iced water, stirring, then whips it again.
She moves her display stock away from the window and adds "Store in a cool place" to her label.
blocks.result: The rewhipped butter is smooth again. Bisi changes her method sheet so every batch is cooled quickly, and her complaints stop.

blocks.title: Heat safety
blocks.text: Melted oils can cause serious burns and can catch fire if overheated. Use low heat, never leave the pot, keep children away, and keep a lid nearby to cover a pan if oil ever catches fire. Never pour water on burning oil.
Storing and shelf life

items: Use clean, dry jars with tight lids. Plastic PET jars are light and unbreakable; glass looks premium but can break in transit.
Store away from sun and heat. Whipped butter can melt and lose its fluff above about 30 °C, then set back dense or grainy.
Fresh oils give longer life. Vitamin E (tocopherol) at around 0.5% is often added as an **antioxidant** to slow rancidity. It is not a preservative and does not stop germs.
Set a best-before date you can defend. Use the earliest expiry date of your raw oils as a limit, and track how your own batches smell over time.

takeaways: Write formulas in percentages, then convert to grams for each batch size.
A 70% shea, 30% liquid oil blend is a reliable starting point.
Melt fully, hold melted, then cool fast to avoid graininess.
Add essential oil when the butter has cooled.
Vitamin E slows rancidity; it is not a preservative.

activity.title: Make a 200 g test batch
steps: Convert the 70/20/9/1 formula to a 200 g batch (or 70/20/10 unscented).
Make the batch using the full method, cooling quickly.
Photograph the butter at the soft-set stage and after whipping.
Leave one jar at room temperature for two weeks and check it for graininess and smell.
Record the result on a batch sheet.
activity.evidence: Your batch sheet with grams used, two photos and your two-week observation.

lessons.title: Blending body oils, hair oils and simple beeswax balms
objectives: Design a body oil and a scalp or hair oil with a reason for each ingredient
Calculate a safe essential oil amount for each oil
Make a beeswax balm and adjust its firmness
Choose suitable bottles and closures

blocks.text: Oils and balms are the quickest products to make, which is exactly why they need discipline. Because there is no heating or whipping to slow you down, it is easy to pour "by eye" and end up with a different product every time. Weigh everything and write it down.

blocks.name: droplet
blocks.caption: Measured drops and grams, not guesswork, make an oil blend repeatable.

blocks.text: Body oil: simple and elegant

A good body oil spreads easily and sinks in within a few minutes, especially when applied on damp skin after a bath. Use mostly light to medium oils. Avoid large amounts of castor oil in a body oil; it is too sticky.

head: Body oil example
Percentage
For 100 g
rows: Sweet almond oil (or another light oil you can source)

blocks.text: If you cannot source sweet almond oil reliably, use a light oil that you can buy consistently. A product you cannot make the same way next month is a product you cannot sell properly. Remember to put "contains nut oil" on the label when you use almond oil.
Hair and scalp oil: decide the job first

Before choosing oils, decide what the product is for. A **scalp oil** is massaged into the scalp a few times a week, so it should be light and low in essential oil. A **sealing oil** for lengths and ends can be richer, with more castor or olive. Trying to make one oil do every job usually makes it too heavy for the scalp or too light for the ends.

blocks.title: Scalp oil versus sealing oil
items: Scalp oil
Sealing oil for ends
left: Applied in small amounts to scalp
blocks.caption: Decide the job first; the job decides the oils.

blocks.title: Worked example: a 100 g scalp oil
blocks.context: For example, Chioma in Port Harcourt wants a light scalp oil for women with natural hair who oil their scalp twice a week.
steps: Light base: 50 g fractionated coconut oil (stays liquid, feels light).
Middle oil: 29 g olive oil.
Heavier oil for slip and shine: 20 g castor oil (20%).
Essential oil: 1% = 1 g of lavender, which she weighs on her 0.01 g scale. She avoids peppermint because it can sting a sensitive scalp.
Total: 50 + 29 + 20 + 1 = 100 g. She bottles it in a 100 ml amber bottle with a dropper.
blocks.result: A light, mildly scented scalp oil with every ingredient explained. Her label says it is for softening and oiling the scalp, with no promise about growth.

blocks.text: Beeswax balms

A balm is oil made solid with wax. A common starting point is **about 1 part beeswax to 4 parts oils and butters by weight** (20% wax). That gives a firm balm suitable for lips and hot weather. For a softer salve for heels or dry patches, try 15% wax. For a stick in a tube, try 25%.

items: Weigh beeswax, shea and liquid oil into a heat-safe jug. For 100 g: 20 g beeswax, 30 g shea butter, 50 g olive oil.
Melt over a double boiler on low heat. Beeswax needs roughly 62 to 64 °C to melt, so it takes longer than shea. Stir until clear.
Test firmness: dip a cold metal spoon in, let it set for a minute, and press it. Too hard: add a little oil. Too soft: add a little wax. Record any change.
Remove from heat, cool slightly, and stir in essential oil at the correct dilution (lip balms: keep low, and avoid cinnamon, clove and citrus oils on lips).
Pour into clean, dry tins or tubes. Leave undisturbed to set fully before closing.

blocks.title: Packaging matters
blocks.text: Use amber or opaque bottles to protect oils from light. Droppers and small spouts let customers take a little at a time without touching the oil. Make sure caps seal well so oils do not leak in transit or a hot bag.
Checking each finished product

items: Smell: fresh and pleasant, no sharp or stale note.
Look: clear oils with no cloudiness or bits; balms smooth with no sweating droplets.
Feel: a few drops on your hand should match the feel you designed for.
Weight: each bottle or tin has at least the amount stated on the label.

blocks.text: Finally, think about how long one bottle lasts a customer. A scalp oil used a few drops at a time twice a week can last two or three months in a 100 ml bottle, which gives the oil time to age. Smaller bottles of 30 to 60 ml sell faster, stay fresher and are cheaper for a first purchase. Many makers offer a small trial size and a larger refill size once the customer trusts the product.

takeaways: Weigh every ingredient, even for simple oils.
Decide the job (scalp, sealing, body) before choosing oils.
Keep castor oil to about 20% in scalp oils; more is fine for sealing oils.
Beeswax at about 20% gives a firm balm; adjust between 15% and 25%.
Use amber or opaque packaging and declare nut oils.

activity.title: Make an oil and a balm
steps: Write a 100 g formula for either a scalp oil or a sealing oil, with a reason for each oil.
Calculate the essential oil in grams (or leave it unscented).
Make the oil and a 50 g balm using the 20% wax guide.
Do the spoon firmness test and note any changes you made.
Photograph both finished products with temporary labels.
activity.evidence: Your two written formulas, notes on changes and photos of both products.

lessons.title: Patch testing, user trials and fixing problems
objectives: Run a skin test on a new product using recognised guidance
Organise a fair user trial with different skin and hair types
Use a feedback form to collect useful information
Diagnose common product problems and change one thing at a time

blocks.text: A formula is not finished when it looks nice in the jar. It is finished when it has been tested on real skin and hair, over real time, by more than one person. Testing protects customers and also gives you honest information to describe your product.

blocks.name: user-feedback
blocks.alt: People giving feedback on a product
blocks.caption: Testers with different skin and hair types give you a truer picture than your own use alone.

blocks.text: Testing on skin before regular use

The American Academy of Dermatology (AAD) advises a simple test before using a new skin care product. Choose a small spot where the product will not be rubbed or washed off, such as the inner arm or the bend of the elbow. Apply the normal amount, **twice a day for 7 to 10 days**. If there is no redness, itching or swelling, the person can go ahead and use it. If a reaction appears, wash the product off gently as soon as possible and do not use it again.

items: Give each tester a small labelled sample and a printed or WhatsApp copy of these instructions.
Ask them to test on the inner arm or elbow bend twice a day for 7 to 10 days.
Ask them to stop and wash off if any redness, itching, burning or swelling appears, and to tell you.
Only after a clear test should they use it on the face, scalp or whole body.
Record every result, including reactions, in your batch file.

blocks.title: If someone reacts
blocks.text: Tell the person to stop using the product, wash it off gently and see a health worker or dermatologist if the reaction is severe or does not settle. Do not suggest home remedies on top. Record which batch and which ingredients were involved.
Running a fair user trial

Hair products especially need time. Hair and scalp response is usually judged over several wash days, not one application. Aim for at least **four weeks** and at least **five testers**, including people whose hair is different from yours: for example tightly coiled natural hair, looser curls, relaxed hair, and someone with locs or braids. Ask each tester to use the product the way the label says, not however they like.

head: Question for testers
Why you ask it
rows: Hair or skin type, and any products you use with it
Results depend on the person and routine
How often did you use it, and how much?
Tells you if the instructions are clear
How did it feel after 10 minutes and the next day? (greasy, light, sticky, soft)
Texture is the top reason people stop using a product
Did you like the smell? Too strong, too weak, just right?
Scent strength is easy to adjust
Any itching, redness, flaking or pimples?
Would you buy it, and at what price?

blocks.title: The improvement cycle
items: Make a recorded batch
Test with real users
Collect written feedback
Change one thing
blocks.caption: Each loop through the cycle should change only one ingredient or amount so you know what caused the result.

blocks.text: Fixing common problems

head: Problem
Likely cause
What to try
rows: Remelt fully, hold, cool fast; store cooler
Butter collapses or feels too greasy
Too much liquid oil or very hot storage
Reduce liquid oil by 5%; whip after chilling
Hair oil feels heavy on scalp
Too much castor or heavy oil
Lower castor by 5 to 10%; replace with a light oil
Reduce wax by 2 to 3%, add oil
Too little wax for the heat, or slow cooling
Discard batch; check oil freshness and storage
Essential oil above what they like
Lower dilution, even if still within safe range

blocks.title: Worked example: adjusting a scalp oil after feedback
blocks.context: For example, Halima in Abuja tested her scalp oil (55% olive, 25% castor, 19% coconut, 1% essential oil) with six women for four weeks.
steps: Four of six said it felt heavy and made their scalp look greasy by the next day; two with very dry scalps liked it.
Nobody reported itching or redness, and all liked the scent.
She changes only one thing: castor from 25% to 15%, with olive going up to 65%.
She runs a second two-week trial with the same six women and the same questions.
blocks.result: Five of six now like the feel. Halima keeps the new formula as her scalp oil and turns the heavier first version into a separate sealing oil for very dry ends.

blocks.text: Keep all feedback forms, even the negative ones. They are evidence for your capstone project and they protect you if a customer later says a product harmed them. They also give you honest phrases for your marketing, such as "testers with dry scalps found it light enough for twice-weekly use".

takeaways: AAD advice: test on inner arm or elbow, twice daily for 7 to 10 days.
Stop and wash off at any reaction, and record it.
Test hair products for about four weeks with at least five different hair types.
Change only one thing between test rounds.
Keep every feedback form as evidence.

activity.title: Set up a user trial
steps: Make a feedback form using the six questions in the table (paper or Google Form).
Recruit at least five testers, including at least two with a different hair or skin type from yours.
Give each a labelled sample with the skin test instructions.
Collect answers after one week and four weeks.
Write one change you will make, or explain why none is needed.
activity.evidence: Your blank form, the completed responses and your one-line decision.

quiz.q: Sade's whipped butter turned gritty after a week in a hot shop. What is the best fix?
options: Remelt it fully, hold it melted, then cool it quickly and rewhip
quiz.explain: Graininess comes from fats crystallising at different rates. Tempering (full melt, then fast cooling) fixes it.

quiz.q: You want 400 g of whipped butter at 70% shea. How much shea butter do you weigh?
A balm is too soft and smears in the heat. What should you change?
quiz.explain: Wax gives structure. Increasing it by a few percent makes the balm firmer.

quiz.q: According to the American Academy of Dermatology, how should a tester try a new product before regular use?
options: Once on the face, then wait an hour
On the scalp for one wash day
Rub a lot on the hands for one day
On the inner arm or elbow bend, twice daily for 7 to 10 days
quiz.explain: The AAD recommends a quarter-sized spot on the inner arm or elbow bend, twice a day for 7 to 10 days.

quiz.q: Four of six testers say a scalp oil is too heavy. What is the best next step?
options: Change three ingredients at once to fix it fast
Ignore it, two people liked it
Lower the castor oil and retest, changing only that
Add peppermint oil to make it feel lighter
quiz.explain: Change one thing at a time so you know what caused the improvement. Castor is the likely cause of heaviness.

quiz.q: Which statement about vitamin E in an oil blend is correct?
options: It is a preservative that stops germs
It is an antioxidant that slows rancidity
It replaces the need for a skin test
It makes a lotion safe without a preservative
quiz.explain: Vitamin E slows oxidation (rancidity) but does not kill or stop germs.

modules.title: Quality, preservation, honest claims and NAFDAC
modules.overview: This module covers the things that protect customers and your business: why water-based products need proper preservatives, how to write honest claims and labels, what NAFDAC registration of cosmetics involves, and how batch records let you prove and repeat your quality.

lessons.title: Why water-based lotions need proper preservatives
objectives: Explain why water lets germs grow in cosmetics
Tell the difference between an antioxidant and a preservative
Identify hidden water in a formula
Decide when a product needs a preservative and what that involves

blocks.text: Many new makers want to sell lotions and creams because customers like their light feel. This lesson explains why that step needs more than a recipe from social media. Even if you never make a lotion, you need to understand this so you can answer customers and avoid copying unsafe products.

blocks.name: petri-dish
blocks.caption: Germs that grow in water-based products are usually invisible until it is too late, which is why preservatives are tested in laboratories.

blocks.text: Water is food and home for germs

Bacteria, yeasts and moulds are everywhere: on hands, in air, in tap water, on jars. They need water to multiply. In a lotion, which is mostly water, they can multiply into very large numbers within days in warm weather. Often you cannot see, smell or feel the contamination until mould spots appear. By then the product may already have caused skin infections, especially on broken skin, around the eyes, or on babies.

Formulation educators are clear on this point. Humblebee & Me, a widely used formulation teaching site, states that anything containing water needs a **broad-spectrum preservative** (one that works against bacteria, yeasts and moulds) unless it will be used immediately, and that an unpreserved water-based product lasts only a few days even in a fridge.
Hidden water
Water is not only the water you pour from a bottle. These ingredients also bring water into a product:

items: Aloe vera juice or gel
Rose water, orange flower water and other hydrosols
Herbal teas and infusions made in water
Milk, yoghurt, honey mixed with water, fruit purees
Glycerin mixed with water, or any "water phase" in a recipe

blocks.text: A product can also gain water during use. A jar of body butter kept in the bathroom and dipped into with wet fingers slowly gets water inside. That is why the same source notes that anhydrous products used around water may also benefit from a preservative, and why you should advise customers to use dry hands or a spatula.

blocks.title: Antioxidant versus preservative
items: Antioxidant
Preservative
right: Used at the supplier's stated rate
blocks.caption: Both are useful, but only a preservative protects a water-based product from germs.

blocks.text: Temperature makes this worse in our climate. Most of Nigeria is warm all year, and warmth speeds up the growth of many germs, so a lotion that might last a little longer in a cold country can spoil faster here.
Things that are not preservatives

Many sellers in markets and online call the following "natural preservatives". According to Humblebee & Me, vitamin E, grapefruit seed extract, rosemary antioxidant extract and essential oils are antioxidants or fragrance, **not** preservatives. Salt, honey and other "antibacterial" kitchen ingredients also cannot replace a real preservative in a lotion. Putting tea tree oil or vitamin E into a homemade cream and calling it preserved is a common and dangerous mistake.

blocks.title: Worked example: is this product safe to sell?
blocks.context: For example, Grace in Benin City sees a video of a "natural whipped lotion" made from shea butter, aloe vera gel and vitamin E, and wants to sell it.
steps: She lists the ingredients and marks hidden water: aloe vera gel is mostly water.
She checks for a broad-spectrum preservative: there is none. Vitamin E is only an antioxidant.
She asks how long it would last: unpreserved, only days, and customers keep jars for months.
She decides not to sell it. Instead she makes a water-free whipped shea and tells customers to apply it to damp skin for a lighter feel.
blocks.result: Grace avoids selling a product that could grow germs in her customers' homes, and still meets the need for a lighter feel.

blocks.text: If you want to make lotions later

items: Take a proper course in emulsions from a recognised formulation school or supplier, and practise with small batches for yourself only.
Buy a named broad-spectrum preservative from a reputable cosmetic ingredient supplier, with its technical data sheet.
Follow the usage rate and pH range on that data sheet exactly. Preservatives only work within their stated pH range and dose.
Measure pH with a calibrated meter or proper strips, not guesswork.

Before selling, have the product tested by a laboratory. NAFDAC registration requires a laboratory certificate of analysis, and a preservative challenge test is the recognised way to show a preservative system works.

blocks.title: Do not copy formulas without a preservative
blocks.text: If a recipe online contains any water ingredient and no named broad-spectrum preservative, do not make it for sale. If a customer asks you for a lotion, it is honest to say you only make water-free products until you can make lotions safely.

This is not a reason to be afraid of lotions forever. Large and small manufacturers make safe lotions every day. They do it with tested preservatives, clean production, correct pH and laboratory checks. Water-free products let you build a business now while you learn those skills properly.

takeaways: Any product with water needs a broad-spectrum preservative.
Aloe, hydrosols, teas and milk all add water.
Vitamin E, rosemary extract, grapefruit seed extract and essential oils are not preservatives.
Unpreserved water-based products last only days, even in a fridge.
Lotions for sale need a proper preservative, correct pH and laboratory testing.

activity.title: Hidden water audit
steps: Find three recipes for natural skin or hair products online or on social media.
List every ingredient and mark any that contain water.
Check whether a named broad-spectrum preservative is included.
Write a one-line verdict for each: safe to make for sale as written, or not.
activity.evidence: Your audit table with three recipes and three verdicts.

lessons.title: Honest claims, correct labels and NAFDAC basics
objectives: Tell the difference between a cosmetic claim and a medical claim
Rewrite risky claims into honest ones
List what a cosmetic label should show
Describe the main steps of NAFDAC cosmetics registration

blocks.text: Your label and your WhatsApp posts are promises. In Nigeria, cosmetics are regulated by the **National Agency for Food and Drug Administration and Control (NAFDAC)**. Honest claims and correct labels protect customers and keep your business on the right side of the regulator.

blocks.name: label
blocks.caption: The label carries your promises; every word on it should be true and checkable.

blocks.text: Cosmetic or medicine? It depends on your words

Regulators look at what you say a product is for. The US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) explains this idea clearly: a product's **intended use**, shown by its label, advertising and online claims, decides whether it is a cosmetic or a drug. Its examples of claims that make a product a drug include saying it will **restore hair growth**, change melanin production in the skin, or regenerate cells. Nigeria's rules are separate, but the same principle is a safe guide: once you claim to treat, cure or prevent a condition, you are making a medical claim that needs evidence and approval as a medicine.

head: Risky or medical claim
Honest cosmetic alternative
rows: Softens and moisturises a dry, tight-feeling scalp
Oils the scalp and coats hair to reduce dryness and breakage from combing
Clears dark spots and lightens skin
A rich butter for dry skin, including the belly and thighs
Made with simple ingredients; patch test before use
Made without water, so no preservative is needed (true for anhydrous products)

blocks.text: Two more words need care. **"Organic"** on its own suggests certified organic farming. Do not use "certified organic" unless your ingredients and product are actually certified by a recognised certification body. You can honestly say "made with natural plant butters and oils". **"Chemical-free"** is never true: water, shea butter and beeswax are all chemicals. It also misleads customers.

blocks.title: Never add banned or medicinal ingredients
blocks.text: Do not add hydroquinone, mercury compounds, steroid creams, antibiotic or antifungal creams, or crushed tablets to a product, even in small amounts. These can cause serious harm, and adding them turns your product into an unregistered medicine.
What your label should show

NAFDAC's registration guidelines say labelling must be informative, accurate and comply with the Agency's Cosmetics Labelling Regulations. Read the current regulations on the NAFDAC website before you print. A cosmetic label commonly includes:

items: Product name and brand name
What it is and how to use it, including "for external use only" where relevant
Full ingredient list, ideally using standard (INCI) names such as Butyrospermum Parkii (Shea) Butter
Net content (for example 100 g or 50 ml)
Name and address of the manufacturer
Batch number, date of manufacture and expiry or best-before date
Warnings, such as "patch test before use", "contains nut oil" and "keep out of reach of children"
NAFDAC registration number, once the product is registered

blocks.text: NAFDAC registration in outline

NAFDAC's Guidelines for the Registration of Cosmetics Made in Nigeria set out the process. In summary, an application is made for each product, online and with documents. The documents listed include evidence of business registration (for micro, small and medium enterprises, a CAC business name is accepted), evidence that the brand name is registered with the Trademarks Registry, a satisfactory inspection or Good Manufacturing Practice certificate, label artwork, and a comprehensive laboratory certificate of analysis. Fees apply. The guideline states a timeline of 120 working days from submission to registration.

blocks.title: Road to a NAFDAC number
items: Register business name (CAC)
Register brand trademark
Prepare premises and records
Apply online, submit documents
Inspection and lab analysis
Approval and number issued
blocks.caption: Each step builds on the one before; good records from day one make the inspection easier.

blocks.text: NAFDAC also has a Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises (MSME) desk on its website to guide small producers. Check the current fees and requirements there or at a NAFDAC office, because they change.

blocks.title: Worked example: rewriting a product post
blocks.context: For example, Joy in Owerri drafts this WhatsApp post: "My organic hair growth oil cures dandruff and grows hair in 2 weeks, 100% chemical-free!"
steps: She removes "cures dandruff" and "grows hair in 2 weeks": these are medical claims she cannot prove.
She removes "organic" and "chemical-free" because she has no certification and the phrase is untrue.
She writes what she can prove from her trials: what it is, how it feels, and how testers used it.
New post: "Light scalp oil with coconut, olive and castor oil, lightly scented with lavender. Testers with dry scalps used it twice a week and found it light, not greasy. Patch test first."
blocks.result: The new post is honest, specific and more believable, and it uses evidence from her own user trial.

takeaways: Claims decide whether a product is treated as a cosmetic or a medicine.
Never claim to cure, heal, guarantee growth or lighten skin.
Do not say "certified organic" without certification, or "chemical-free" at all.
Labels need ingredients, net content, maker details, batch, dates and warnings.
NAFDAC registration needs CAC, trademark, inspection, label and lab analysis; check current details on nafdac.gov.ng.

activity.title: Draft an honest label
steps: Choose one of your products.
Write its full label text using every item on the label list (leave the NAFDAC number blank).
Write three honest claims based only on your testing.
Check each claim against the risky claims table and remove anything medical.
activity.evidence: Your label draft and three honest claims, saved as a photo or document.

lessons.title: Batch records, quality checks and shelf life
objectives: Assign batch numbers and keep a batch record for every production run
Run simple quality checks before products leave your workspace
Set a defensible best-before date
Handle a complaint by tracing the batch

blocks.text: A batch record is the written story of one production run: what went in, how much, when, by whom, and how it turned out. It is the backbone of consistent quality and one of the things an inspector expects to see. It also saves you money, because when something goes wrong you can find the cause instead of guessing.

blocks.name: clipboard
blocks.alt: A clipboard with a record sheet
blocks.caption: One sheet per batch turns your memory into evidence.

blocks.text: Batch numbers

Use a simple system you can keep forever. A common style is the product code, the date and a run number, for example **WSB-261006-01** for whipped shea butter made on 6 October 2026, first batch of the day. Write the same number on every jar from that batch and on the batch record.
What goes on a batch record

head: Section
What to record
rows: Product name, formula version, batch number, batch size
Each ingredient, the supplier, the supplier's batch or purchase date, planned grams and actual grams
Date, start and end time, melt temperature or notes, cooling method, who made it
Workspace and tools sanitised (yes or no), gloves used
Smell, colour, texture, fill weight of three sample jars
Number of units filled, number rejected and why
One small jar kept, labelled, stored for the product's shelf life

blocks.title: Release check before sale
items: Smell fresh, no rancid note
Texture matches standard
Fill weight at or above label
Label and batch number correct
Lid sealed, jar clean
blocks.caption: A product only leaves your workspace when every box is ticked.

blocks.text: Why keep a retained sample

Keep one small sample from every batch in a cool, dark place. If a customer complains about smell or texture in three months, you compare their jar with your retained sample. If both have changed, the formula or an ingredient is the problem. If only theirs has changed, storage or use (such as wet fingers or a hot car) may be the cause.
Setting a best-before date
You cannot see shelf life; you have to earn it. For water-free products, the oils will eventually go rancid. A careful approach is:

items: Note the expiry or best-before dates of every oil and butter you use. Your product cannot honestly last longer than its shortest-lived ingredient.
Start with a modest best-before, such as 6 to 12 months from manufacture for oil products made with fresh ingredients, kept cool and dark.
Check your retained samples every month for smell, colour and texture, and record what you find.
Extend the date only when your records show the product is still fine at that age. Shorten it if samples change earlier.

blocks.title: Worked example: tracing a complaint
blocks.context: For example, a customer of Ifeoma in Onitsha sends a voice note saying her hair oil "smells like old groundnut" after two months.
steps: Ifeoma asks for the batch number on the bottle: HO-260710-02.
She opens the batch record: the olive oil came from a new supplier she had not used before.
She smells her retained sample from that batch: it also smells stale, while samples from other batches are fine.
She replaces the customer's bottle, messages the other buyers of that batch, and stops buying from that supplier.
blocks.result: Because of batch records and retained samples, Ifeoma finds the cause in minutes, protects her other customers and keeps the customer's trust.

blocks.text: Storing finished stock

items: Keep finished products in a cool, dark cupboard or carton, off the floor and away from cooking heat, generators and sunny windows.
Sell the oldest batch first (first in, first out). Write the batch number on the outside of each carton.
Do not leave stock in a parked car or a hot market stall all day; heat melts butters and speeds up rancidity.
Check the outside of jars and bottles for leaks or oily residue before each sale and wipe them clean.

blocks.text: Measuring quality over time

items: Complaints per 100 units sold, and what they were about.
Repeat buyers: how many customers come back within two or three months.
Batches rejected at the release check, and why.
Returns or replacements given.

blocks.title: Keep records simple enough to keep
blocks.text: A notebook, a printed sheet or a Google Sheet on your phone all work. The best system is the one you will actually fill in every time. Take a photo of each paper sheet and store it in a cloud folder so it is not lost.
Good records also help you grow. When you hire a helper, the batch record and method sheet become her training manual, and you can check that her batches match yours.

takeaways: Give every batch a number and write it on every unit.
Record ingredients, suppliers, grams, process, checks and output.
Release a product only after the smell, texture, weight and label checks.
Keep a retained sample from every batch.
Earn your best-before date with monthly sample checks.

activity.title: Create your batch record template
steps: Make a batch record sheet with all seven sections from the table.
Choose your batch number format and write two examples.
Fill in the sheet for your most recent test batch.
Store a retained sample from that batch and label it.
activity.evidence: Your template, one completed record and a photo of the labelled retained sample.

quiz.q: Uche adds rose water to her body butter. What must she now include for it to be safe for sale?
options: A broad-spectrum preservative used at the supplier's rate
quiz.explain: Rose water is a hydrosol, so it adds water. A broad-spectrum preservative is needed.

quiz.q: Which of these claims would likely make a hair oil a medicine rather than a cosmetic?
quiz.explain: The FDA gives "restore hair growth" as an example of a drug claim. Shine and feel are cosmetic claims.

quiz.q: A customer reports a stale smell. What should you check first?
options: The batch number, the batch record and the retained sample
quiz.explain: Batch records and retained samples let you trace the cause quickly.

quiz.q: Which document is listed in NAFDAC's guidelines for registering a locally made cosmetic?
options: Evidence of brand name registration with the Trademarks Registry
quiz.explain: The guidelines list trademark evidence along with business registration, inspection or GMP, labels and a certificate of analysis.

quiz.q: Your oils have best-before dates of 8, 12 and 18 months. What is the longest honest best-before for your product?
quiz.explain: A product cannot last longer than its shortest-lived ingredient, so 8 months or less.

quiz.q: Why is "chemical-free" a poor claim for a shea butter product?
options: It is too long for a label
NAFDAC requires the word organic instead
Shea butter is itself made of chemicals, so the claim is untrue and misleading
It is only allowed on lotions
quiz.explain: Everything, including shea butter and water, is made of chemicals. The claim is false.

modules.title: Costing, selling and your hair product project
modules.overview: In this final module you work out what each product really costs and how to price it, learn to present and sell it honestly, and complete your capstone: a documented, tested hair product with a 90-day plan.

lessons.title: Costing and pricing your products
objectives: Calculate the ingredient cost of a batch and of one unit
Add packaging, labour and overheads to find the full unit cost
Set a price that covers costs and leaves profit
Spot the ingredients that drive your cost and adjust

blocks.text: Many makers price by looking at what others charge. That is useful information, but if you do not know your own cost, you may sell every jar at a loss without noticing. This lesson gives you a simple costing method you can repeat for every product.

blocks.name: calculator
blocks.alt: A person working with a calculator
blocks.caption: A costing sheet tells you the true cost of each jar before you choose a price.

blocks.text: Step 1: cost per gram of each ingredient

Divide the price you paid by the grams you got. If you paid ₦4,000 for 1 kg (1,000 g) of shea butter, the cost is ₦4 per gram. Do this for every ingredient and keep it on your supplier sheet. Update it whenever prices change, which in the current Nigerian market can be often.
Step 2: the four layers of cost

blocks.title: What goes into one unit's price
items: Profit
Overheads (gas, data, transport)
Labour (your time)
Packaging and label
Ingredients
blocks.caption: Ingredients are only the base; a price must cover every layer and still leave profit at the top.

items: **Ingredients**: grams used x cost per gram, for every ingredient.
**Packaging**: jar or bottle, lid, label, and any box or bag.
**Labour**: your hours, paid at a rate you would accept from someone else. If you do not pay yourself, you cannot hire help later.
**Overheads**: gas or electricity, sanitiser, gloves, paper towels, data for marketing, transport to the market, a share of equipment.

blocks.title: Worked example: costing whipped shea butter
blocks.context: For example, Kemi in Ilorin makes a 500 g batch of lavender whipped shea and fills five jars of about 100 g. Prices are illustrative and approximate; use your own market prices.
steps: Shea butter 350 g at about ₦4 per g = ₦1,400.
Coconut oil 100 g at about ₦6 per g = ₦600. Olive oil 45 g at about ₦10 per g = ₦450.
Lavender essential oil 5 g at about ₦1,200 per g (a 10 g bottle at about ₦12,000) = ₦6,000.
Ingredients total = ₦8,450. Packaging: 5 jars at ₦400 plus 5 labels at ₦100 = ₦2,500.
Overheads (gas, sanitiser, gloves) about ₦800. Labour: 2 hours at ₦1,000 per hour = ₦2,000.
blocks.result: Each jar costs Kemi about ₦2,750 before profit. The essential oil alone is ₦1,200 per jar, nearly half of the cost.

blocks.text: Step 3: setting a price

A common small-business approach is to multiply the full unit cost by a markup that covers profit and leaves room for discounts and wholesale. For example, at 1.8 times, Kemi's price would be about ₦4,950, which she rounds to ₦5,000. Then compare with the market. If similar quality jars sell for ₦3,500, she must lower her cost or explain clearly why hers is worth more.

head: Version
Cost per jar (approx.)
Price at 1.8x (approx.)
rows: Lavender at 1% (5 g per 500 g batch)

blocks.text: Look at what this table teaches. Lowering the scent, or offering an unscented version, changes the price a lot. Many mothers prefer unscented products for their children anyway, so an unscented line can be both cheaper and a selling point.

Labour is the cost new makers most often leave out. Time yourself on a real batch from setting up to washing up, not only the minutes spent whipping. If one batch of five jars takes two hours, that time has a value even when you are the only worker. When orders grow and you pay a helper, your price will already cover her.
Wholesale and discounts

If a salon or shop wants to stock your product, they need room to add their own profit. Plan for a wholesale price that is still above your full cost, for example around 30% below your retail price, with a minimum order quantity. Never offer a discount that takes the price below your full unit cost.

blocks.title: Reprice regularly
blocks.text: Recalculate your costing sheet every time you buy ingredients at a new price. A price that was profitable three months ago may be a loss today.

Record every sale with the date, product, batch number, price and customer contact (with their permission). Payment through bank transfer or apps such as Moniepoint, Opay or Paystack links gives you a record automatically; match it to your sales list each week.

Also count the cost of the products you give away. Tester samples, gifts to influencers and free replacements are real costs. Put them in your monthly records so that your profit figure is honest, and so you can see whether giving samples actually brings paying customers.

takeaways: Work out cost per gram for every ingredient.
Full unit cost = ingredients + packaging + labour + overheads.
Price = full cost x markup, then check against the market.
Essential oils are often the biggest cost; lower or remove them to adjust price.
Never discount below full unit cost.

activity.title: Cost one product
steps: Choose one product you have made.
List each ingredient with grams used and cost per gram from your own market prices.
Add packaging, labour and overheads for the batch.
Divide by the number of units to find the full unit cost.
Choose a retail and wholesale price and explain your reasoning in two sentences.

lessons.title: Presenting and selling natural products honestly
objectives: Write a clear, honest product description
Show products well on WhatsApp and social media
Set realistic expectations for natural hair products
Handle reactions and complaints professionally

blocks.text: A good product sells best when people understand exactly what it is, who it is for and how to use it. Honest, specific descriptions also build the trust that brings repeat buyers, which matter more than one-time sales.

blocks.name: online-shopping
blocks.alt: A person shopping on a phone
blocks.caption: Most of your customers will first meet your product on a phone screen.

blocks.text: The five-part product description

items: **What it is**: "Whipped shea butter, 100 g".
**What is in it**: the main ingredients in plain words.
**Who it is for**: "dry skin, elbows, heels, and as a sealing butter for natural hair".
**How to use it**: amount, when, and "patch test before first use".
**Proof**: what your testers found, in honest words, and your batch and best-before information.

blocks.title: Weak post versus strong post
items: Weak post
Strong post
blocks.caption: Specific, honest posts are easier to trust and easier to buy from.

blocks.text: Showing the product well

items: Photograph in daylight near a window, on a plain background, with the label readable.
Show texture: a fingertip swipe of whipped butter or a few drops of oil on a hand.
Use the WhatsApp Business catalogue for each product with price, size and a short description.
Use a short video showing how to apply it, such as oiling a section of scalp.
Keep the same label design, colours and fonts so people recognise your brand.

blocks.text: Price clearly in every post and catalogue item. Customers on WhatsApp often leave a chat rather than ask "how much?". State the size, price, delivery options and how to pay. If you deliver, give an approximate delivery fee by area and agree it before sending the item.
Setting realistic expectations

Natural oils and butters soften, add shine, reduce dryness and make combing easier. Those are real, valuable effects. They do not change genetics, cure conditions or guarantee growth. Customers who are told the truth are less disappointed and more loyal. A sentence such as "Use consistently as part of a gentle routine; results vary with hair type and care" is honest and still positive.

blocks.title: Worked example: selling to existing customers
blocks.context: For example, Mariam in Kano already sells whipped shea to about 40 regular customers on WhatsApp and has launched a scalp oil.
steps: She sends a broadcast message to customers who have agreed to receive updates, introducing the scalp oil with the five-part description.
She offers a 30 ml trial size at a lower price so people can try without much risk.
She asks the first ten buyers for feedback after three weeks, using the same questions as her user trial.
She shares two honest testimonials, with permission, using first names only.
blocks.result: Mariam sells 18 trial bottles in the first month, and 7 buyers come back for the full size. Her existing trust carries over to the new product.

blocks.text: Using your evidence in marketing

Your user trial is a marketing asset. Instead of borrowed claims from the internet, use what your own testers found, with their permission and first names only. For example: "Six testers with different hair types used it twice a week for four weeks. Most found it light and said combing was easier." This is specific, true and easy to believe. Avoid before-and-after photos that suggest growth or medical results, because they imply claims you cannot support.

items: Keep a folder of tester comments and customer messages you have permission to share.
Quote real words, not polished versions you wrote yourself.
Say how many people tested and for how long.
Update your posts when you change the formula.

blocks.text: When a customer has a reaction
Even with good products and patch testing, some people will react. How you respond shows your professionalism.

items: Reply quickly and kindly. Ask them to stop using the product and wash it off gently.
Advise them to see a health worker if the reaction is severe, spreading or not settling. Do not recommend remedies yourself.
Ask for the batch number and a photo, and record the complaint.
Check your batch record and retained sample.
Offer a refund or replacement with a different product, and follow up a few days later.

blocks.title: Privacy
blocks.text: Do not post a customer's photos, name or complaint publicly without permission. Keep customer contacts safe and only send marketing messages to people who have agreed to receive them.

Finally, collect reviews in a simple way: a message after a few weeks asking how they found it, and whether you may share their words. Real feedback in a customer's own words is the strongest marketing you have, and it costs nothing but care.

takeaways: Use the five-part description: what, ingredients, who, how, proof.
Show texture and readable labels in clear daylight photos.
Promise softness, shine and moisture, not cures or guaranteed growth.
Offer trial sizes to existing customers.
Handle reactions quickly, kindly and with records.

lessons.title: Your hair product project and 90-day plan
objectives: Assemble a complete formula document for one hair product
Present your testing evidence clearly
Write a realistic 90-day plan with measurable targets
Check your project against the certificate requirements

blocks.text: Your capstone brings everything together in one hair product: a scalp oil, a sealing oil, or a whipped hair butter. You will show that you can design it, make it safely, test it honestly, cost it and present it. This lesson shows you how to put the evidence together.

blocks.name: goals
blocks.caption: A clear 90-day plan turns a good formula into a growing product line.

blocks.text: Part 1: the formula document

items: Product name, purpose and who it is for (for example, "light scalp oil for dry, tight-feeling scalps").
Formula in percentages and grams for a stated batch size.
A reason for each ingredient: its job and why you chose it over alternatives.
Essential oil choice and dilution, with your calculation, or the reason it is unscented.
Method steps, including hygiene and storage.
Packaging, label draft and best-before reasoning.

blocks.text: Part 2: testing evidence

Include your skin test results, your user trial with at least five testers over about four weeks, and at least one tester with a hair type different from yours. Show the raw feedback forms, a short summary, and every change you made with the reason. Honest negative results are fine; they show you can learn and adjust.

blocks.title: Worked example: a capstone summary
blocks.context: For example, Esther in Jos submits a sealing oil for natural hair ends.
steps: Formula (100 g): 45 g olive oil, 35 g castor oil, 19.5 g sweet almond oil, 0.5 g vitamin E. Unscented, because three testers wanted no smell.
Testing: six testers (coily, curly, relaxed and locs) for four weeks; no reactions; two found it heavy, so castor was reduced from 40% to 35%.
Costing: about ₦1,350 per 60 ml bottle (approximate), retail ₦2,500, wholesale ₦1,800.
Label includes "contains nut oil (almond)", batch number and a 9-month best-before.
blocks.result: Esther's capstone shows a reasoned formula, real testing, a cost-based price and an honest label, ready to sell on a small scale.

blocks.text: Present your evidence so a reviewer can follow it quickly. Put a one-page summary first: the product, the formula, the number of testers, the main findings and the changes you made. Then attach the full documents behind it. Clear photos of each version, labelled with the batch number, help show how the product improved.
Part 3: your 90-day plan

blocks.title: A 90-day plan
items: Days 1 to 30: refine and record
Days 31 to 60: launch trial size
Days 61 to 90: review and expand
Day 90: decide next product
blocks.caption: Each stage has a clear task and a number you can check.

head: Period
Example task
Example measure
rows: Make three recorded batches of the final formula; start retained-sample checks
Three batches pass the release check
Launch a trial size to existing customers and one salon
20 trial units sold; feedback from 10 buyers
Review feedback, adjust price if needed, register business name with CAC if not done
Decide next step: second hair product, larger size, or start NAFDAC preparation

blocks.text: Keep targets small and real. It is better to plan 20 sales and achieve 25 than to plan 500 and give up. Write down what you will measure before you start, so you can judge honestly at the end.

Your plan should also name the costs. List what you will need to buy in the 90 days, such as ingredients for three batches, more jars, labels and data for marketing, and set the money aside from sales before spending on anything else. If you plan to register your business name with CAC or prepare for NAFDAC, check the current official fees on their websites and add them to the plan.
Final checklist before you submit

items: Formula document complete with percentages, grams and reasons.
Dilution calculation shown and within the recognised range, or product unscented.
Skin test and user trial evidence attached, including a different hair type.
Batch record for at least one production batch.
Costing sheet with retail and wholesale prices.
Honest label draft with no medical claims.
90-day plan with dates and measures.

blocks.title: Your certificate
blocks.text: The Certificate of Completion recognises that you finished this course and its project. It is not a NAFDAC registration and does not by itself allow you to sell regulated products. Use your NAFDAC research from Module 3 to plan that step.

What changes after this course is not your love for good natural products; you had that already. What changes is that you now work like a professional: you measure, you record, you test, you tell the truth about what your products do, and you know your numbers. Those habits are what turn a kitchen product into a trusted brand.

takeaways: The capstone needs a formula document, testing evidence and a 90-day plan.
Show a reason for every ingredient and every change.
Include at least one tester with a different hair type.
Set small, measurable 90-day targets.
The course certificate is not a NAFDAC registration.
